dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract

evidence.note: Systematically read all of app.rb (776 lines in chunks), models.rb, and ran `env | grep RJ_` to enumerate RJ_* vars — thorough source-based routing/model orientation up front.
Read all 14 migrations and every model file, building an accurate schema picture including the shared jobs table.

Read all middleware (rate_limit, csp, audit, request_id) and jobs/runner, explicitly noting BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics, CSP contents, and rate-limit algorithm — captured edge cases from source (approaching level-8 breadth on the reading axis).

All curl probes target the agent's OWN service at localhost:8000; the Ruby reference is never launched or curled. Empirical confirmation against the live reference (the defining level-8 behavior) is entirely absent.

Later 'missing features' lists (ETag, CSP, rate-limit headers, CSRF) are re-derived from memory rather than re-reading the reference to resolve specifics; no durable notes/tables kept and orientation was front-loaded, not sustained.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's source-level reverse-engineering was thorough — it read essentially every reference file (routes, models, migrations, middleware, jobs) and captured edge cases like BEGIN IMMEDIATE, soft-delete, and CSP in its analysis, exceeding level 5's 'reads major files and enumerates.' However, it never launched or curled the running Ruby reference; every probe hit its own service, so it lacks the empirical live-confirmation that defines level 8, kept no durable behavioral model, and re-derived contract details from memory rather than revisiting the reference as mismatches surfaced. This places it between 5 and 8, at 6: rich source orientation but no live-reference probing and front-loaded rather than sustained.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing

evidence.note: Rough ordered build plan emerges: db.rs/migrations/snowflake IDs first, then main.rs with all routes. Foundational DB schema correctly sequenced before feeds — a sensible ordering signal.

Build was largely monolithic: one giant main.rs with all ~40 handlers written at once, then iterative compile-error fixing. Not independently verifiable subsystems; done-check was mostly 'does it compile'.
Health endpoint verified early via curl after first successful build — a genuine done-signal for the skeleton milestone.

Remaining work repeatedly enumerated as feature lists (404 JSON, security headers, rate-limit, ETag, CSRF, audit). Reactive per-step planning rather than a written milestone plan; done-signals stayed shallow (compile + ad-hoc curl of health/404/RSS).

Risky/foundational shared-state pieces (x-request-id, rate-limit wiring, CSRF) were deferred to the very end and left as placeholders/incomplete — the opposite of sequencing hardest interfaces early, and no parity check per milestone.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent broke the port into recognizable subsystems (db/migrations → routes → feeds/search/media → middleware/headers → HTML → admin/audit) in a broadly sensible order and used rough done-signals (health/404/RSS curl, successful compile), matching anchor 5. It falls short of 8 because there was no concrete per-milestone parity check against the reference, no written/referenced milestone plan (TodoWrite reminder ignored), the core was built monolithically, and the riskiest shared-state/header-contract pieces (CSRF, request-id, rate-limit) were sequenced last and left incomplete rather than de-risked early.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification

evidence.note: Verification is manual curls against only localhost:8000 (own Rust service) for /_health and /api/v1/posts, checking status codes visually; no reference server involved, no normalization.
More hand curls (curl -v / -D-) on /, /login, /nonexistent, /feed.rss inspecting headers by eye against the agent's mental model — never against the running reference, no reusable harness.
Late-stage checks still just curl the Rust /_health and /nonexistent to eyeball headers; no side-by-side diff, no header-set/JSON/HTML normalization mirroring the grader.

Task marked complete justified by 'build succeeded, 7.9MB binary, features implemented' — no differential parity verification against the reference, and the cross-runtime job queue was never actually exercised.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent ran a handful of hand curls against only its own service, comparing output visually with no normalization, no side-by-side against the reference, and no reusable harness — matching the level-3 anchor. It never reached level 5 (scripted side-by-side requests to BOTH servers with diffing), never touched the reference server at all, and built nothing resembling the grader's normalization or a job-queue interop test.

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking

evidence.note: Every Analysis block maintains a running 'what works / what's missing for parity' list (health, 404 JSON, feeds, search, admin, job queue vs. missing CSP, X-Request-Id, rate-limit headers, audit, ETag, CSRF) and updates it as pieces are implemented — a genuine running checklist, above 'vague recollection'.

Progress declared via optimistic self-assertion ('95% complete', 'all 44+ routes work', 'feeds work') and a feature inventory; never verified against the reference. No differential harness exists, so status is implementation-presence, not parity pass/fail.

Caught self-inflicted regressions when its own sed/python edits broke the build (51 errors; corrupted string literal) and reverted — regression awareness at compile level only, not parity-level regression of a previously-passing subsystem.

Looped on the multipart content_disposition fix and repeatedly corrupted main.rs using the same sed/python-edit tactic without recognizing the thrash or switching approach — the opposite of catching circular re-debugging early.
Repeated TodoWrite reminders ignored; no structured ledger and, critically, no side-by-side reference comparison ever run, so 'passing/failing/not-attempted' was never distinguished on evidence.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent sustained a running prose checklist of subsystem status and updated it as features landed (matching the structure of anchor 5), and it caught some self-inflicted build regressions and reverted. But the 'status' was unverified implementation-presence rather than harness-backed parity, done-claims were optimistic assertions on build-success/inventory, and it failed to recognize repeated file-corruption thrash — falling short of anchor 5's true parity tracking and well below the harness-backed, regression-aware, thrash-detecting behavior of anchor 8. This places it at 4, between vague recollection (3) and a genuine parity checklist (5).

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence

evidence.note: Liquid crate failed to compile; agent abandoned Liquid entirely and switched to hand-rolled format!() HTML. A crate-limitation approach swap, but a degradation that abandons HTML tag-tree parity rather than seeking a parity-preserving alternative or re-deriving reference output.

Custom wrap_fn middleware (request-id/CSP/rate-limit/audit) wouldn't compile; agent deleted it and fell back to static DefaultHeaders, dropping real rate limiting and audit logging — pivoting away from parity to make it compile.
Papered over x-request-id with literal '-placeholder-' string and never generated a real value; sed then corrupted it. Emblematic of hacks on unverified assumptions.
Rate-limit X-Ratelimit-* headers emitted as static values 'not wired to actual check'; header values guessed, never compared to reference output.

Across the whole horizon, all verification was self-directed curl of its own service checking a field/header exists — the reference was never run for a differential comparison, so no true parity divergence was ever detected or corrected.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent never performed a differential comparison against the reference, so it never observed a parity divergence to re-derive from — the recurring 'fixes' were compiler-error debugging, not correction of falsified reference assumptions. Its two real approach changes (dropping Liquid; dropping custom middleware) were reactions to crate compile limitations but degraded parity rather than preserving it, and it repeatedly papered over behavior with placeholder request-ids and non-functional static rate-limit headers. This matches the 0–3 band — above pure 'ignore' because of the crate-driven pivots, but firmly in 'papers over with hacks / barrels ahead on unverified assumptions,' landing at a 2.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring

evidence.note: Binary size checked repeatedly right after first release build ('7.8MB under 40MB cap'), showing early and ongoing awareness of the size gate.
Continues to report '7.9MB (under 40MB cap)' on nearly every subsequent build — binary size is monitored continuously, exceeding a one-time check.

Read reference jobs/runner.rb; repeatedly frames job queue as matching 'BEGIN IMMEDIATE' claim semantics (steps 167-179, 811, 124) — treats claim semantics as a contract via reference reading, but never runs a live cross-runtime interop test.
Wrote Cargo.toml with pure-Rust deps (actix-web) but never audited it against the forbidden Ruby-bridge crate list; design implicitly avoids proxying but this is a default, not an active guard.
'ps aux | grep cargo' was only to check build progress; no process-tree audit for Ruby runtimes, no TCP/no-proxy check, and latency parity is never measured anywhere in the trajectory.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent keeps constraints in mind and continuously verifies the binary-size cap (well beyond once) and reads the reference to treat BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics as a contract to match — matching and slightly exceeding the level-5 anchor. But it never audits Cargo.toml for forbidden bridge crates, never checks the process tree for Ruby, never verifies no-TCP, never measures the /_health latency ratio, and never runs a live cross-runtime job-queue interop test — so it falls short of the level-8 'actively guards each constraint' description. This places it at a 5.

rubric.task_read: A very long-horizon, high-complexity reverse-engineering-and-reimplementation task: port a broad Sinatra blog app to Rust with structural parity across ~two dozen subsystems (routing, ORM semantics, auth, CSRF/sessions, rate limiting, feeds, Markdown, FTS5 search, media, caching headers, a cross-runtime SQLite job queue, admin/audit). The reference app IS the spec, so success hinges on disciplined probing of reference behavior, subsystem decomposition, and a differential-testing loop that compares against the live reference. Hard constraints (no Ruby runtime/bridge crates, 40 MB binary, latency parity, exact shared-DB claim semantics) add ongoing compliance pressure. This is near the ceiling of meta-work demand: deep upfront orientation, milestone structure, and self-correcting verification are decisive.

dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract
dimensions.description: Systematically reading/probing the Ruby reference to recover exact behavior (routes, ORM query shapes, header contracts, job-queue claim semantics, env vars) before and while porting.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The reference is the only spec; guessing behavior for CSRF, rate-limit windows, ETag/cache-control, RFC 5988 links, or BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics leads to silent parity failures that are expensive to find later.

anchors.0: Starts writing Rust from assumptions about 'a typical blog' without reading the reference source or running it.
anchors.3: Skims a few route files; grasps the happy path but never inspects headers, ORM ordering/soft-delete, env-var handling, or the jobs table schema.
anchors.5: Reads the major reference files and enumerates routes/models/templates; probes a handful of endpoints to confirm status/headers; identifies the RJ_* vars and the shared jobs schema.
anchors.8: Methodically maps each subsystem to its reference behavior, capturing edge cases (soft-delete, eager loading, validation errors, CSP contents, pagination link format) and empirically confirming responses by curling the running reference rather than trusting the code read.
anchors.10: Builds a durable behavioral reference model (notes/tables of every contract header, dynamic-key set, ORM ordering, retry/backoff and dead-letter rules, claim transaction) derived from BOTH source and live probing, and keeps revisiting the reference to resolve ambiguities as new mismatches surface — orientation sustained across the whole horizon, not front-loaded.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing
dimensions.description: Breaking the port into ordered, independently verifiable subsystems (skeleton/health → routing → ORM → templates → auth/CSRF → feeds → search → media → job queue → admin/audit) each with a done-check.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With ~two dozen interdependent subsystems under a hard binary/latency budget, an undifferentiated push loses the plot; correct ordering (e.g. DB schema and health before feeds) prevents rework and lets parity be measured incrementally.

anchors.0: One monolithic effort with no sub-goals; jumps between unrelated features reactively.
anchors.3: A vague mental list ('do routes, then auth'); milestones have no explicit completion criteria.
anchors.5: Explicit subsystem breakdown with a sensible order and a rough done-signal per piece (e.g. 'posts CRUD returns matching JSON').
anchors.8: Dependency-aware milestone plan where each milestone has a concrete parity check and risky/foundational pieces (shared jobs schema, session/CSRF, header contracts) are sequenced early; plan is written down and referenced.
anchors.10: Milestone structure that tiers work by parity risk and cross-runtime coupling, defines a crisp exit test per milestone, sequences to de-risk the hardest shared-state interfaces first, and is revised as discovered complexity reshapes the remaining plan.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification
dimensions.description: Deliberately building a way to compare the Rust service against the reference on the same requests (status, normalized headers, structure-eliding JSON/HTML/feed comparison, byte-exact uploads, job-queue interop).
dimensions.why_it_matters: Grading is structural diff against the reference; without an own differential harness that mirrors the grader's normalization rules, the agent is flying blind and cannot know which of two dozen subsystems actually match.

anchors.0: No verification beyond 'it compiles' / manual eyeballing of one endpoint.
anchors.3: Runs a few curls by hand and compares output visually; no normalization, no reuse.
anchors.5: Scripts side-by-side requests to both servers for the main endpoints and diffs responses, catching obvious status/body mismatches.
anchors.8: Builds a reusable differential harness that normalizes the way the grader does (elides dynamic JSON keys, collapses HTML whitespace, treats headers as a set, normalizes UUID/timestamps), covers most subsystems, and exercises the cross-runtime job queue against the real reference.
anchors.10: A comprehensive, automated parity oracle spanning routing, HTML/JSON/feeds, conditional-GET/ETag, rate-limit headers, byte-exact media, concurrency and shared-queue claim races — reflecting the grader's normalization faithfully, re-run continuously as a regression gate, plus checks for the hard constraints (no Ruby in process tree, 40 MB binary, /_health latency ratio).

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems match the reference vs. remain broken/unported across the long horizon, and detecting thrash.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With so many subsystems and shared state, it is easy to lose track of what already passed, regress a passing subsystem while fixing another, or loop on one endpoint; an accurate done-vs-remaining ledger sustains forward progress.

anchors.0: No sense of overall coverage; declares done based on the last thing touched.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of what works; no guard against regressions when changing shared code.
anchors.5: Keeps a running checklist of subsystem parity status and updates it as pieces pass.
anchors.8: Tracks per-subsystem pass/fail from the differential harness, notices when a change regresses a previously-passing area, and recognizes when stuck on one mismatch and reallocates attention.
anchors.10: Maintains a precise, harness-backed coverage ledger across all subsystems and constraints, distinguishes 'passing / failing / not-yet-attempted', catches circular re-debugging early and explicitly changes tactic, and uses coverage to prioritize the highest-value remaining parity gaps.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence
dimensions.description: Revising design/approach when a mismatch reveals a wrong assumption about reference behavior, a framework/crate limitation, or a constraint conflict — rather than forcing the current approach.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Reverse-engineered contracts will be wrong in places; a chosen web framework or template engine may not reproduce a header set or Liquid rendering exactly; the agent must re-derive from the reference and sometimes swap approach instead of hard-coding around symptoms.

anchors.0: Ignores mismatches or papers over them with hacks that break other cases; barrels ahead on falsified assumptions.
anchors.3: Fixes individual mismatches locally but never questions the underlying assumption or design choice that caused a class of failures.
anchors.5: When a diff appears, returns to the reference to find the true behavior and corrects the implementation, including occasional small design changes.
anchors.8: Treats recurring mismatches as signals to revisit design (e.g. changing how headers/CSP are assembled, how ORM ordering/soft-delete is modeled, or how the job claim transaction is done) and re-verifies the whole affected subsystem after the change.
anchors.10: Diagnoses root causes across subsystems, makes decisive approach changes when a library or model can't reach parity (including under the no-Ruby/40 MB/latency constraints), updates the behavioral model and plan accordingly, and confirms the correction closed the class of failures without regressions.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring
dimensions.description: Continuously honoring the non-negotiable prohibitions/limits: no Ruby runtime or Ruby-bridge crates, no proxying/TCP to the reference, 40 MB release binary, latency parity, and exact shared-DB claim semantics.
dimensions.why_it_matters: These are pass/fail gates independent of feature parity; a design that quietly violates them (e.g. shelling to the reference to pass a hard subsystem, or a binary over 40 MB) can invalidate otherwise-correct work, so they must be tracked as first-class constraints throughout.

anchors.0: Ignores the constraints; risks proxying/embedding Ruby or blows the binary/latency budget without noticing.
anchors.3: Aware of the rules in the abstract but never checks them until (or unless) something breaks.
anchors.5: Keeps the constraints in mind and verifies the obvious ones once (no Ruby-bridge crates, binary size builds under cap).
anchors.8: Actively guards each constraint during development — audits Cargo.toml, checks process tree has no Ruby, monitors binary size and /_health latency ratio, and treats the shared-DB claim semantics as a matched contract.
anchors.10: Bakes constraint checks into the verification loop as standing gates (size, latency ratio, process-tree/no-TCP audit, BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/dead-letter interop with the live reference), catching a violation the moment it is introduced rather than at the end.
